S001.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
S001.description: Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes.
examples: Makes mistakes in homework or tests by misreading questions or skipping important parts.
Frequently omits details or makes typos in work documents or reports.
Repeats mistakes in calculations or numerical work, such as switching signs or getting digits wrong.
Performs tasks incorrectly by missing important details in instructions.

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
examples: Desk, bag, or room is always messy and remains disorganized.
Unable to prioritize or determine the order of tasks, starting them randomly.
Fails to plan time effectively, frequently missing deadlines or rushing to finish at the last minute.
Feels overwhelmed by how to start multi-step projects and procrastinates.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
examples: Continually procrastinates or is reluctant to start writing long reports or complex homework.
Avoids activities that require long periods of concentration, such as reading books or studying.
Passes off tasks that require complex thinking or planning to others.
Gets annoyed or resists when asked to start a task that requires significant mental effort.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
examples: Easily distracted and stops working due to small noises or movements nearby.
Cannot concentrate because eyes keep wandering to the scenery outside the window or people passing by.
Starts daydreaming or gets sidetracked by sudden thoughts while working or studying.
Loses focus and listens in when hearing side conversations or TV sounds.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
examples: Forgets appointment times or meeting schedules, arriving late or missing them entirely.
Forgets to reply to received calls or messages for days.
Frequently incurs late fees because of missing deadlines for utility bills or credit card payments.
Forgets to take medication or leaves necessary items at home when going out.

S015.name: Excessive_Talking
examples: Talks incessantly and cannot tolerate silence, continuing to chatter.
Continues to talk even when others are bored or try to cut the conversation short.
Talks too much inappropriately for the situation, making people around them uncomfortable.
Monopolizes the conversation and gives almost no chance for others to speak.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation) is characterized primarily by persistent patterns of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus, disorganization, forgetfulness, and frequent careless errors, without prominent hyperactive or impulsive behaviors. Onset is typically in childhood, but it is often unrecognized until academic, occupational, or role demands exceed the individual’s compensatory strategies, leading to clear functional impairment in adulthood. The course is usually chronic, with fluctuating impact depending on structure, support, and environmental demands. It is distinguished from anxiety, depression, and normal distractibility by its early onset, cross-situational persistence, and specific cognitive-attentional deficits rather than mood or situationally limited problems.

patient.personality: Keisy is a detail-focused and conscientious planner who enjoys structure and self-improvement, yet tends to overcommit to projects and become absorbed in her interests to the point of losing track of time and routine obligations.
patient.stressor: Nearly two years ago, Keisy’s manufacturing plant expanded production and tightened quality benchmarks, which meant more simultaneous inspection lines, increased documentation requirements, and frequent protocol updates she was expected to learn and then teach to newer staff. In the past she had managed her tendency to get absorbed in conversations or hobbies by using rigid personal routines, but the accelerating pace of changes at work and the need to constantly shift attention between stations, emails, and training duties strained those coping strategies. Over the ensuing months, she noticed that informal mentoring sessions and discussions on the floor would run long, leaving her scrambling to complete logs and reports, and that after work she often lost large chunks of time tinkering with new recipes or side projects she had optimistically scheduled for the same weekend. As her supervisor began pointing out recurring delays in documentation and she herself grew frustrated with how her time seemed to slip away from her, particularly when she was talking with colleagues or friends, she sought psychiatric help hoping to understand why managing her focus and follow-through felt so much harder despite her efforts to stay organized.
patient.chief_complaint: “Once I get talking with people, I go on and on and then I realize I’ve lost track of time and what I was supposed to be doing.”

S001.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
S001.description: Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes.
S001.manifestation: Lately my supervisor keeps circling little things in my inspection logs—like I’ll type the wrong lot number or skip a checkbox—even though I swear I went over them, it’s like my eyes just glide right past the small details when I’m a bit rushed or tired.

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
S005.manifestation: When they roll out a new protocol and I’m supposed to learn it, update my notes, schedule time to train the newer staff, and still cover two lines, I just stare at my planner not knowing what to tackle first, so I end up bouncing between tasks and then scrambling at the end of the shift.

S006.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
S006.description: Often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort.
S006.manifestation: If I know I have to sit down and really focus on a long email about a new procedure or write up a detailed incident report, I’ll keep putting it off with little excuses—checking on a line, tidying my station, even scrolling my phone—because the idea of that sustained concentration feels exhausting.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
S008.manifestation: On the floor I’ll be halfway through checking a batch and then a coworker laughs across the room or a thought about a new recipe pops into my head, and suddenly I’m mentally somewhere else and have to backtrack to remember where I was in the inspection.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
S009.manifestation: Outside of work I’m constantly apologizing because I forget to call people back, leave my meal prep groceries sitting on the counter until things spoil, or miss an online bill until I get the reminder email and realize I spaced it completely.

S015.name: Excessive_Talking
S015.manifestation: At work and with friends, once I get going explaining something—like a new protocol or some random project I’m into—I just keep talking and adding details, and only notice I’ve gone on way too long when I see people glancing at the clock or trying to jump in.
